title: Japanese accepted-answer additions — author evidence, second version
status: revised after one independent review; the revisions have not themselves been reviewed

input.note: A proposal is a candidate, not a correction.

grader.call: lib/grading.ts gradeAnswer, with the runtime exerciseHints from lib/exercise-restore.ts (exerciseType, skillType, targetGrammar, targetWord, language: "ja")
grader.bar: An addition counts as accepted only when the feedback is exactly "Correct!".
grader.before_values: re-derived against the frozen snapshot, after the grading.ts and confusable-pairs.ts changes of 2026-09-14; recorded before-values were not reused.

per_alternative_against_the_1163_propose.note: One entry per (row, candidate) pair. Every figure in this file uses this base; the first version mixed it with a distinct-decision-unit base, which the review caught.

additions_not_named_by_any_proposal.note: Candidates no proposal named on that row: the first taken from a sibling row sharing the gloss and key, the second added on review so every person row carries all five persons.

counts.reconciliation: 738 accepted proposals + 10 sibling harmonisations + 14 person harmonisations = 762 additions on 428 rows.

readmission.first_version: opened 8 new entries inside the guard scope and 79 readmissions in the wider scope, 29 of them meaning flips.
readmission.this_version: zero, in the guard scope and in the wider scope. Replayed against the current draft plus this batch: 71 found, 71 declared, none new, none Japanese. The batch test now carries the same measurement in a scope strictly wider than the shipped guard, so it cannot regress.
readmission.mechanism: gradeAnswer measures typo distance against whichever accepted answer is NEAREST the input, so every addition carries a ball of radius min(2, floor(min(len(addition), len(key)) * 0.3)).
readmission.why_a_pair_on_the_key_is_inert: isConfusablePair is consulted against the matched alternative, not the key, so lib/confusable-pairs.ts already declaring the whole もっと+adjective set changed nothing once an addition was the nearest string. Any pair must be keyed on the ADDED string.

confusable_pairs_required.note: The pairs that would let the withdrawn typo-ball and self-contradiction additions be restored, keyed on the ADDED string as the mechanism requires. NOT written into lib/confusable-pairs.ts: that file has a concurrent owner and is read-only to this agent. Pairs would not undo the register, meaning or overt-pronoun withdrawals, which are content decisions rather than grader artefacts.
confusable_pairs_required.shape_limit: Derived by restoring every withdrawn addition and measuring, so a pair appears only when at least one member is an addition of this batch. Collisions between two STORED KEYS are outside that shape by construction and are listed separately under preexisting_collisions_not_caused_by_this_batch; the two antonym pairs of that kind, To fire / To hire and 背が高い / 背が低い, were added to the pair list by the integration owner. ["Granddad","Grandpa"] is not listed because both are withdrawn together and a restoration pass restores them together, onto the same row, where neither can readmit the other.

preexisting_collisions_not_caused_by_thi.note: Rows of the FROZEN Japanese curriculum that already grade a sibling unit key correct with no patch of any kind, measured after the integration owner added the two antonym pairs. All 17 are one shape: a fill_blank completion key — a suffix such as ました, べき, ーズ, ぶん — sitting inside the typo ball of the whole word on a sibling row. None is a meaning flip. Pairs are the wrong remedy here, because each of these suffixes is the legitimate stored key of its own fill_blank row; scoping completion keys out of the sibling-key pool is. Recorded for the owner of that decision, not acted on.

policies.script: No addition turns on how the same word is written; such candidates are withdrawn to the open JA-KANA-KANJI-SCRIPT question. Enforced on review for とびら, which granted a second orthography of an added lexeme.
policies.politeness_and_register: A candidate that is the plain or casual counterpart of a polite key is refused, whether or not it is the same lexeme. Made uniform on review.
policies.within_typo_ball: An addition is withdrawn when a sibling key, a sibling addition, or a string this batch itself withdraws in the same unit sits within the grader’s edit budget of it, min(2, floor(min(len(addition), len(key)) * 0.3)). Stated by that metric rather than as a minimal pair, which the first revision got wrong.
policies.transcription: dictation and listening_type rows are out of scope.
policies.sibling_consistency: Rows sharing an English gloss and a stored key carry identical additions; the person ground carries all five persons on every row.
policies.contamination: No addition is the stored key of another Japanese row under a different English gloss, nor a distractor on a sibling choice row built on the same stimulus.

refusal_grounds.script_variant: Same lexeme, different orthography (kana for a kanji spelling or the reverse, the other kana, a variant kanji, okurigana moved). Withdrawn to the open JA-KANA-KANJI-SCRIPT policy question, not judged wrong.
refusal_grounds.politeness: Differs from the key only in politeness (plain vs ます/です). The course encodes register in the English gloss and the A2 units carrying these rows are named for the form being drilled.
refusal_grounds.register: The casual counterpart of a polite key — the same speech act at a lower politeness level, lexeme or not. Made uniform after review: the batch refuses 55 candidates for swapping politeness and the reconciliation holds おはようございます -> おはよう on that ground, so ごめん for すみません, うん for はい, ううん for いいえ and the ちゃん forms of さん kinship terms go the same way.
refusal_grounds.drilled_form: Swaps the tense, aspect or finiteness the row is drilling. The A2 units are "Past Tense Basics" (ました) and "Future Plans" (します); the gloss selects the form.
refusal_grounds.course_distinction: The course keys this string to a different English gloss elsewhere, or a sibling choice row on the same stimulus offers it as a distractor. Accepting it collapses a distinction the curriculum teaches.
refusal_grounds.not_an_answer: Not an answer to this row: a fragment, a particle that is not the word, or a bound form the stem cannot take on its own.
refusal_grounds.different_sense: A narrower, wider or different sense from the one the prompt glosses, or a bare form whose reading is ambiguous.
refusal_grounds.minimal_pair: A minimal pair of a sibling key or of a sibling addition inside a unit whose content IS a set of minimal-pair contrasts. The addition is correct; admitting it makes the unit’s own contrast unmarkable, because the grader forgives anything inside the typo ball of the nearest accepted entry. The remedy is a confusable pair keyed on the ADDED string; the pairs are listed in confusable_pairs_required below and the addition is withdrawn until they land.
refusal_grounds.overt_pronoun_withdrawn: 私は + the keyed form is correct Japanese, but it lands on seven cloze_deletion rows that ask for one missing word, and the three past-tense forms are mutually one edit apart so each row admitted the other two verbs. Withdrawn uniformly so sibling rows do not disagree.
refusal_grounds.self_contradiction: The batch refuses or withdraws this string elsewhere and then readmits it through the typo ball of an addition on the same row.

acceptance_grounds.lexical: an ordinary Japanese equivalent of the stored key, with nothing in the bare prompt narrowing the sense
acceptance_grounds.english: an ordinary English rendering of the same sense, and the prompt supplies no context that selects the keyed wording
acceptance_grounds.kinship: Japanese kinship, in-group and beautified vocabulary comes in own-side, other-side and honorific pairs, and a bare English gloss selects none of them
acceptance_grounds.completion: the visible stem admits this completion as well as the keyed one, and the prompt selects neither
acceptance_grounds.person: a subjectless Japanese predicate does not specify person, and the prompt names no subject
acceptance_grounds.idiom: a standard equivalent of the same figurative meaning; the learner is asked to translate the idiom, not to reproduce one fixed form

additions_that_already_pass_through_edit.note: Already marked correct today, but only as a "minor typo" of the key, so the learner is shown the key as a correction of their own correct answer. Each is a different Japanese form, not a typo. Bears on remediation/runtime-independent-review/confusable-pairs-cjk.md.

uncertain_triage.note: Triaged, not adjudicated. Verified by the review, every number.
what_would_settle_it: One decision, not 371: should grading compare Japanese answers by reading rather than by string? If yes, the fix is reading-aware normalisation in lib/grading.ts, not 357 accepted_answers edits; if no, 350 rows close as correct as stored.

283 of the 371 are dictation or listening_type rows, where the prompt IS the Japanese word and the learner types what they heard, so rejecting kana there measures IME conversion rather than comprehension.

The current draft already answers yes on exactly one row: ja-E2267 (listening_type, key 受身) has うけみ added, exact_value_independently_approved. Verified by the review. One row granted and 350 refused is the inconsistency to resolve.
The 9 rows carrying JA-POLITE-AFFIX close without the script decision: they are the register question this batch answers against, and the review forced that answer to be uniform.

limits: Authored by one agent and revised against one independent review. The revisions have not themselves been reviewed.

Judgements rest on the author’s reading of each row against its prompt, key, lesson, unit and sibling rows in the frozen snapshot. No per-candidate dictionary lookup was performed and no source is cited for an individual call.
The minimal-pair withdrawals remove correct answers. They are withdrawals pending the 39 confusable pairs, not judgements that the strings are wrong.
Graded against the frozen snapshot. Only ja-E2267 of the 552 is touched by the draft, and it is emptied here.
